subject: St Martin of Tours

text_used.text: Every quotation below is checked word for word against Alexander Roberts's unrevised translation (NPNF 2nd series vol. 11, 1894), downloaded whole from CCEL. 'exact' is the translation as printed, with its footnote numbers taken out. 'display' applies the site's rule of capitals for every pronoun for God. Where New Advent's revised copy differs, the note says how.
text_used.source: Alexander Roberts (tr.), Sulpitius Severus, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894), CCEL plain-text copy, marked Public Domain
text_used.note: New Advent modernises the archaic forms (thee/thy/thou/ye become you/your) and drops some question marks, e.g. 'Brictio?' becomes 'Brictio.'. Chapter links below go to CCEL's chapter pages, all checked (HTTP 200, right heading). In Roberts the Dialogues are three (I, II, III), the same as New Advent's split. The Latin editions and the New Catholic Encyclopedia count two, so Roberts's Dialogue II is their 'Dialogue 1 (2)' and his Dialogue III is their 'Dialogue 2 (3)'.

born_place.text: Born at Savaria (Sabaria) in Pannonia, today Szombathely in Hungary. Raised at Ticinum, today Pavia in Italy. His parents were pagans.
born_place.source: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St Martin, chapter 2 (Roberts: 'born at Sabaria in Pannonia, but was brought up at Ticinum'); Catholic Encyclopedia (1910), 'St. Martin of Tours' (Szombathely)
born_place.note: The Szombathely identification comes from the Catholic Encyclopedia and the New Catholic Encyclopedia, not from Sulpicius.

born_year.text: About 316. Some scholars put it about 336. The sources disagree.
born_year.source: New Catholic Encyclopedia, 2nd ed., 'Martin of Tours, St.' (H. G. J. Beck), via Encyclopedia.com: 'b. Sabaria ... c. 316', and 'scholars differ in the matter of Martinian chronology'. Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks 1.36: born 'In the eleventh year of his reign' (Constantine's). Sulpicius, Dialogue II, chapter 7: served at the empress's table 'when in his seventieth year' (Maximus's court, about 385).
born_year.note: The 336 date: Wikipedia's note says Clare Stancliffe, St. Martin and His Hagiographer (1983), pp. 119-133, prefers 336. I did not see the book. The Episcopal Church's Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 says 'about 330'. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1910), OCA and Britannica say 316. Plain wording that holds: 'Born about 316 (some scholars say 336)'.

died.text: Died 8 November 397 at Candes, a village in his diocese of Tours, of a fever in old age. Buried at Tours three days later, on 11 November.
died.source: New Catholic Encyclopedia ('d. Candes, Nov. 8, 397'; burial at Tours three days later); OCA, 'Saint Martin the Merciful, Bishop of Tours' ('died on November 8, 397. He was buried three days later (his present Feast) at Tours'); Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks 1.48 (Brehaut tr., 1916): 'departed this life at Candes, a village of his diocese ... in the eighty-first year of his life and the twenty-sixth of his episcopate', 'at midnight of the Lord's day, in the consulship of Atticus and Cæsarius'; Sulpicius, Letter 3 (the fever)
died.note: No ancient text I read gives the day '8 November'. Gregory gives the year (the consuls Atticus and Caesarius mark 397), a Sunday, and midnight. By my own calculation, 8 November 397 in the Julian calendar was a Sunday, so the two agree. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) says 'most probably in 397' and notes that some authorities give 400. Sulpicius calls the place 'Condate'. Roberts's footnote guesses Cosne, but Gregory of Tours names Candes.

roles.text: Soldier: forced into the army at fifteen, he served in the imperial guard cavalry, first under the emperor Constantius and then under Julian, who was then Caesar.
roles.source: Life of St Martin, chapter 2. Latin (Halm, The Latin Library): 'inter scolares alas sub rege Constantio, deinde sub Iuliano Caesare militavit'
roles.note: Roberts's English says 'enrolled in the imperial guard, first under king Constantine'. The Latin says Constantius, and 'scolares alae' are guard cavalry units. So 'cavalryman' on the site is supported by the Latin.

roles.text: Exorcist under Hilary, bishop of Poitiers.
Monk: founded a monastery near Poitiers (Ligugé), perhaps the first in Gaul, and later Marmoutier outside Tours.
roles.source: Life of St Martin, chapters 7 and 10 (the places are not named there); Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) and New Catholic Encyclopedia name Ligugé and Marmoutier; Britannica: 'Ligugé, the first monastery in Gaul'
roles.note: The New Catholic Encyclopedia is more careful: 'what may have been the first French monastery'. Use 'perhaps the first'.

roles.text: Bishop of Tours from 371 until his death in 397.
roles.source: New Catholic Encyclopedia ('consecrated bishop, probably on July 4, 371'); Britannica ('In 371 he was made bishop of Tours'); OCA (371)
roles.note: The Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) says 371 or 372, consecrated on 4 July. Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 says 372. The 1916 Roman Martyrology keeps 4 July as the anniversary of his elevation to bishop.

also_called.text: Martin the Merciful (OCA, and the Russian Church: 'Мартин Милостивый').
also_called.source: OCA, 'Saint Martin the Merciful, Bishop of Tours': 'He is called the Merciful because of his generosity and care for the poor'; azbyka.ru, 'Святитель Мартин Милостивый, епископ Турский'
also_called.note: Greek sources call him differently: 'Όσιος Μαρτίνος ο θαυματουργός επίσκοπος Φραγκιάς', the Venerable Martin the Wonderworker, bishop of Frankia (saint.gr).

catholic.text: 11 November (a memorial in the General Roman Calendar). The 1916 Roman Martyrology also keeps 4 July for the moving of his body and the dedication of his church at Tours.
catholic.source: USCCB readings page 'Memorial of Saint Martin of Tours, Bishop' (11 November 2025); The Roman Martyrology (1916), 11 November and 4 July
catholic.note: The 1916 Martyrology on 4 July: 'At Tours, the translation of St. Martin, bishop and confessor, and the Dedication of his Basilica, which took place on the anniversary of his elevation to the episcopate some years previous.' Copy at archive.org/details/romanmartyrology00cathuoft. I did not check the current (2004) Martyrology.

orthodox.text: Churches differ. Greek synaxaria keep 12 November. The Russian Church keeps 12 October on the old calendar, which is 25 October on the civil calendar. OCA keeps 11 November and also lists 12 October. OCA's own Life says the October date 'appears to be an error, since ancient sources give the November date.'
orthodox.source: Great Synaxaristes (synaxarion.gr): 'Ὁ Ὅσιος Μαρτῖνος', 12 Νοεμβρίου; saint.gr: 'Εορτάζει στις 12 Νοεμβρίου'; azbyka.ru: 'День памяти 25 октября'; OCA pages 'Commemorated on November 11' and 'Commemorated on October 12'
orthodox.note: The research notes' clash (12 November or 12 October) is settled: both are real, in different churches. 12 November is the Greek date and 12 October the Slavic date. Other URLs: https://www.synaxarion.gr/gr/sid/1160/sxsaintinfo.aspx ; https://www.saint.gr/3013/saint.aspx ; https://azbyka.ru/days/sv-martin-milostivyj-turskij ; https://www.oca.org/saints/lives/2016/10/12/205432-saint-martin-the-merciful-bishop-of-tours . GOARCH could not be checked: goarch.org answered 403 and then a bot check, which I did not get round.

old_calendar_note.text: Churches on the old (Julian) calendar keep the same date 13 days later on today's calendar: 12 November falls on 25 November, 11 November on 24 November, and 12 October on 25 October.
old_calendar_note.source: azbyka.ru gives 25 October for the Russian 12 October; the 13-day gap holds from 1900 to 2099
old_calendar_note.note: The +13 for 12 October is checked directly. The other two are the same arithmetic.

anglican.text: 11 November. It is a Lesser Festival in the Church of England ('Martin, Bishop of Tours, c.397'), and also kept in the Episcopal Church ('Martin of Tours, Bishop, 397').
anglican.source: Church of England, Common Worship calendar (printed in roman type, which marks a Lesser Festival); The Episcopal Church, Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, calendar and p. 504
anglican.note: Episcopal PDF: https://www.episcopalchurch.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/Lesser-Feasts-and-Fasts-2022_final.pdf . It says: 'Martin died on November 8, 397, but he has long been commemorated on November 11, the date of his burial.'

lutheran.text: 11 November. The Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod lists 'Martin of Tours, Pastor' in Lutheran Service Book.
lutheran.source: LSB commemorations calendar (copy at goodshepherd.nb.ca); The Lutheran Witness (LCMS), 'Saints: More Than a Short List', November 2008
lutheran.note: ELCA (Evangelical Lutheran Worship) could NOT be checked in an ELCA document. Wikipedia and a synod video title give 'Martin, Bishop of Tours, died 397' on 11 November. Tidbit, same LCMS article: Martin Luther got his name 'directly from the saint's day on which he had been baptized, Nov. 11'.

status.text: A saint in the Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches, and commemorated by Lutherans. He was one of the first saints honoured who did not die as a martyr.
status.source: Britannica, 'St. Martin of Tours': 'he was one of the first nonmartyrs to be publicly venerated as a saint'
status.note: Britannica does not say 'in the West'. Keep it general, or say 'one of the first saints honoured who was not a martyr'. His disciple put it this way in Letter 2 (exact): 'although the character of our times could not ensure him the honor of martyrdom, yet he will not remain destitute of the glory of a martyr'.

patron_of.text: France. Britannica adds soldiers and tailors.
patron_of.source: New Catholic Encyclopedia ('patron of France'); Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 ('one of the patron saints of France'); Britannica ('the patron saint of France, soldiers, and tailors')
patron_of.note: Neither the Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) nor the 1916 Roman Martyrology lists a patronage for him. The 1916 Martyrology's patron list has no Martin entry. Wikipedia's long list (beggars, geese, innkeepers, vintners, horses, Buenos Aires, Utrecht, Szombathely, the Swiss Guard and more) is not verified here.

in_art.text: Most often shown cutting his cloak with his sword to share it with a beggar, usually on horseback. El Greco's painting and the Paris icon both show this.
in_art.source: El Greco, Saint Martin and the Beggar (NGA); Petit Palais record PPP4870: 'en selle sur un cheval richement arnaché, le saint s'apprête à couper son manteau avec son épée pour le partager avec le mendiant'
in_art.note: Honest detail: Sulpicius (Life, chapter 3) never mentions a horse. The horse comes from the artists.

in_art.text: A goose, in some later art and in Martinmas customs. This rests on a legend.
in_art.source: Wikipedia, 'Martin of Tours' (it cites a church web page that is now dead); New Liturgical Movement (2022) on the legend
in_art.note: The goose as an emblem in art is not verified from a reliable source. If used, mark it as legend.

in_art.text: A globe of fire over his head. The story is in the Dialogues: at the altar, 'we beheld a globe of fire dart from his head'.
in_art.source: Sulpicius, Dialogue II, chapter 2 (story verified); use as an art attribute per Wikipedia's infobox (not verified)
in_art.note: The story is verified. That artists use it as his sign is not verified.

life_moments.title: The cloak at Amiens
life_moments.text: One bitter winter, at the gate of Amiens, a man with no clothes begged, and everyone walked past him. Martin had already given away his other clothes, so he cut his soldier's cloak in two with his sword and gave the man half. That night he dreamed of Christ wearing that half. Christ said to the angels, 'Martin, who is still but a catechumen, clothed Me with this robe.'
life_moments.source: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St Martin, chapter 3
life_moments.note: Exact in Roberts: 'Martin, who is still but a catechumen, clothed me with this robe.' The quotation keeps 'Me' capitalised for Christ. Some bystanders laughed at him, and others 'groaned deeply because they themselves had done nothing similar'. Roberts gives his age at baptism as twenty, but the Latin says eighteen ('annorum duodeviginti'), so leave the age out.

life_moments.title: Leaving the army
life_moments.text: Before a battle near Worms, Julian, then Caesar, was handing out a bonus to his men. Martin asked to leave instead: 'I am the soldier of Christ: it is not lawful for me to fight.' Called a coward, he offered to stand unarmed in front of the battle line the next day. The enemy asked for peace first.
life_moments.note: Exact full saying in Roberts: 'Hitherto I have served you as a soldier: allow me now to become a soldier to God: let the man who is to serve thee receive thy donative: I am the soldier of Christ: it is not lawful for me to fight.' The Latin is 'Christi ego miles sum: pugnare mihi non licet.' Sulpicius names the city of the Vangiones (Roberts misprints 'Vaugiones'), and Roberts's footnote identifies it as Worms. Julian was Caesar, not yet emperor. The New Catholic Encyclopedia dates the discharge to 356 on one reading, but the dating is disputed.

life_moments.title: Hilary of Poitiers
life_moments.text: Free of the army, he went to Hilary, bishop of Poitiers. Hilary wanted to make him a deacon, but Martin kept saying he was unworthy. So Hilary made him an exorcist, a lowly office Martin would not refuse in case he seemed to look down on it.
life_moments.note: Roberts: 'when he constantly refused, crying out that he was unworthy'.

life_moments.title: Ligugé
life_moments.text: He then spent years away. He went home to Pannonia to win over his mother and fought the Arians. He was driven out of Milan and lived on an island off Italy. When Hilary came back from exile, Martin followed him and set up a monastery near Poitiers. It may have been the first in Gaul.
life_moments.source: Life of St Martin, chapters 6-7; the place is named Ligugé by the Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) and the New Catholic Encyclopedia ('at Ligugé, 8 kilometers south of Poitiers ... c. 360-361 what may have been the first French monastery')
life_moments.note: Sulpicius says only 'a monastery not far from the town'. The name Ligugé comes from later sources.

life_moments.title: Made bishop of Tours
life_moments.text: Tours wanted him as its bishop, but he would not leave his monastery. So a citizen threw himself at his knees and said his wife was ill. Martin came out, and crowds along the road led him into the city. A few bishops said he looked shabby and his hair was a mess. The people laughed at them and had their way.
life_moments.note: The citizen's name: Roberts has 'Ruricius'. Halm's Latin has 'Rusticius', and so does the Catholic Encyclopedia (1910). Leave the name out, or use Rusticius. The bishops said he was 'a man despicable in countenance, that his clothing was mean, and his hair disgusting'. He was bishop from 371; see quick facts.

life_moments.title: Marmoutier
life_moments.text: As bishop he still lived as a monk. When the crowds of visitors grew too much, he built a hidden monastery about two miles outside the city, in a wooden cell between a cliff and the Loire. About eighty disciples lived there. They owned nothing, and the older monks spent their time in prayer.
life_moments.source: Life of St Martin, chapter 10; named Marmoutier ('Majus Monasterium') by the Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) and the New Catholic Encyclopedia
life_moments.note: Exact: 'This spot was so secret and retired that he enjoyed in it the solitude of a hermit.' 'There were altogether eighty disciples.'

life_moments.title: Before the emperor Maximus
life_moments.text: At the court of the emperor Maximus in Trier, the other bishops flattered him. Martin would not. He begged Maximus not to put the followers of the heretic Priscillian to death. He said that being put out of the Church was punishment enough, and that a secular ruler should not judge a church case. Once, to save men already sentenced to death, he took communion for one day with the bishops who had pressed for the executions. He grieved over it for the rest of his life and never went to a synod again.
life_moments.source: Life of St Martin, chapter 20; Sacred History, Book 2, chapter 50; Dialogue III, chapters 11-13
life_moments.note: Other URLs: Life 20: https://ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf211/npnf211.ii.ii.xxi.html ; Sacred History 2.50: https://ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf211/npnf211.ii.vi.ii.l.html . At a banquet he passed the emperor's cup to his own priest, 'as thinking no one worthier to drink next to himself' (Life 20). He opposed Priscillian's teaching. His quarrel was with the killing. Do NOT quote Roberts's next sentence in Sacred History 2.50 ('as long as Martin survived ... when he was about to leave this world'). It mistranslates the Latin 'quoad usque Martinus Treveris fuit ... mox discessurus', which means 'as long as Martin was at Trier ... when about to leave'. Dialogue III.13 says he lived sixteen years after the communion episode. That does not fit a death in 397, which is one reason the dates are disputed.

life_moments.title: His death at Candes
life_moments.text: Old and ill, he travelled to Candes to make peace among its quarrelling clergy. He knew his end was near. Once they were reconciled, his strength failed. He died there, lying on sackcloth and ashes, and would not let his disciples put straw under him.
life_moments.source: Sulpicius Severus, Letter 3 (to Bassula); Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks 1.48
life_moments.note: Sulpicius was not there. In Letter 2 he hears of the death from 'Two monks ... from Tours', and in Letter 3 he tells Bassula to ask 'those who were present'. A good tidbit, but a late one: Gregory of Tours, writing about 590, says the people of Poitiers and Tours fought over the body. At midnight the men of Tours passed it out of a window and took it by boat down the Vienne and the Loire to Tours (History of the Franks 1.48, Brehaut tr., https://sourcebooks.fordham.edu/basis/gregory-hist.asp).

framing.text: Martin wrote nothing that survives. These are his words as his disciple Sulpicius Severus recorded them.
framing.source: New Catholic Encyclopedia: 'The confessio formerly attributed to him is not considered authentic.'
framing.note: In the Dialogues, Martin's sayings come through a speaker (Gallus or Postumianus) in a conversation Sulpicius wrote about 404.

lines.exact: I am the soldier of Christ: it is not lawful for me to fight.
lines.display: I am the soldier of Christ: it is not lawful for me to fight.
lines.note: Said to Julian Caesar. Identical in New Advent. The popular form 'I am a soldier of Christ. I cannot fight' (e.g. Lesser Feasts and Fasts) is a paraphrase.

lines.exact: The Lord Jesus did not predict that he would come clothed in purple, and with a glittering crown upon his head. I will not believe that Christ has come, unless he appears with that appearance and form in which he suffered, and openly displaying the marks of his wounds upon the cross.
lines.display: The Lord Jesus did not predict that He would come clothed in purple, and with a glittering crown upon His head. I will not believe that Christ has come, unless He appears with that appearance and form in which He suffered, and openly displaying the marks of His wounds upon the cross.
lines.note: Said to the devil, who appeared dressed as a king and claimed to be Christ. Sulpicius says he had this 'from the lips of Martin himself'.

lines.exact: If Christ bore with Judas, why should not I bear with Brictio?
lines.display: If Christ bore with Judas, why should not I bear with Brictio?
lines.note: A saying 'he often repeated' about his own abusive priest (St Brice, later his successor). New Advent ends it with a full stop.

lines.exact: See, [says he,] she has fulfilled the precept of the Gospel: she had two coats, and one of them she has given to him who had none: thus, therefore, ye ought also to do.
lines.display: See, she has fulfilled the precept of the Gospel: she had two coats, and one of them she has given to him who had none: thus, therefore, ye ought also to do.
lines.note: Said on seeing a sheep just shorn. Roberts interrupts it with 'says he'. New Advent has 'you ought' for 'ye ought'.

lines.exact: O Lord, if I am still necessary to thy people, I do not shrink from toil: thy will be done.
lines.display: O Lord, if I am still necessary to Thy people, I do not shrink from toil: Thy will be done.
lines.note: His prayer when his disciples begged him not to leave them. New Advent: 'your people ... your will'.

lines.exact: It is not fitting that a Christian should die except among ashes; and I have sinned if I leave you a different example.
lines.display: It is not fitting that a Christian should die except among ashes; and I have sinned if I leave you a different example.
lines.note: When they asked to put straw under him. Identical in New Advent. It is already the site's line for 'the body'.

lines.exact: Why do you stand here, thou bloody monster? Thou shalt find nothing in me, thou deadly one: Abraham's bosom is about to receive me.
lines.display: Why do you stand here, thou bloody monster? Thou shalt find nothing in me, thou deadly one: Abraham's bosom is about to receive me.
lines.note: HIS LAST WORDS. Letter 3 says 'As he uttered these words, his spirit fled.' They are spoken to the devil. New Advent: 'you bloody monster? You shall find nothing in me, you deadly one'. The words just before, to a priest: 'Allow me, dear brother, to fix my looks rather on heaven than on earth, so that my spirit which is just about to depart on its own journey may be directed towards the Lord.'

more_if_needed.exact: The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do unto me.
more_if_needed.note: To the devil on the road past Milan. He is quoting Psalm 118:6.

more_if_needed.exact: If thou, thyself, wretched being, wouldst but desist from attacking mankind, and even, at this period, when the day of judgment is at hand, wouldst only repent of your deeds, I, with a true confidence in the Lord, would promise you the mercy of Christ.
more_if_needed.note: To the devil. Sulpicius hedges: 'Martin is said to have cried out in words to the following effect'. So print it as reported, not verbatim.

more_if_needed.exact: Let the church both feed and clothe us, as long as we do not appear to have provided, in any way, for our own wants.
more_if_needed.note: To his hungry, ragged monks, after he had given away a gift of silver.

more_if_needed.exact: This [exclaimed he] is a picture of how the demons act: they lie in wait for the unwary and capture them before they know it: they devour their victims when taken, and they can never be satisfied with what they have devoured.
more_if_needed.note: On seeing water-birds diving for fish, on his last journey.

others_on_him.exact: No one ever saw him enraged, or excited, or lamenting, or laughing; he was always one and the same: displaying a kind of heavenly happiness in his countenance, he seemed to have passed the ordinary limits of human nature.
others_on_him.note: Already on the site ('calm', 'laugh'). Latin: 'unus idemque fuit semper'.

others_on_him.exact: in Martin alone, apostolic authority continued to assert itself.
others_on_him.note: About the court of Maximus. Latin: 'in solo Martino apostolica auctoritas permanebat'.

others_on_him.exact: Never did a single hour or moment pass in which he was not either actually engaged in prayer; or, if it happened that he was occupied with something else, still he never let his mind loose from prayer.
others_on_him.note: Alternatives, all exact: 'O truly blessed man in whom there was no guile--judging no man, condemning no man, returning evil for evil to no man!' (Life 26). 'a man clearly worthy of being compared to the Apostles' (Sacred History 2.50). 'For who ever suffered but Martin suffered along with him?' (Letter 2).

misquoted_or_legend.claim: He hid among geese to escape being made bishop, and their honking gave him away. This is said to be the origin of the Martinmas goose.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: A later legend. Sulpicius tells a different story: a citizen pretended his wife was ill to get Martin out of his monastery.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Life of St Martin, chapter 9 (read); New Liturgical Movement, 'Saint Martin of Tours: The Man and His Feast' (2022): 'A later legend claims ... betrayed by a honking flock of geese'
misquoted_or_legend.note: The legend's absence from Sulpicius is checked. When and where the goose story began is not.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: He gave only half his cloak because the other half belonged to the Roman army.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Sulpicius does not say this. He says Martin had nothing left but the cloak, 'for he had already parted with the rest of his garments for similar purposes'.
misquoted_or_legend.note: Where the army explanation comes from is not verified.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: When he woke, his cloak was whole again.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Not in Sulpicius, who says nothing of the cloak being restored. Britannica tells it inside a 'Legend holds' paragraph.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Life of St Martin, chapter 3; Britannica ('When he awoke, the garment was restored.')

misquoted_or_legend.claim: He was riding a horse when he met the beggar.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Sulpicius never mentions a horse. Painters added it.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: He said it to the emperor Julian the Apostate.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Julian was then Caesar, a junior ruler, not yet emperor. Sulpicius writes 'Julian Cæsar'. The site's hook already says 'the future emperor Julian'.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Life of St Martin, chapters 2 and 4

misquoted_or_legend.claim: Martin's own writings or sermons, or his 'Confession of Faith'.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Nothing he wrote survives. The confession of faith once credited to him is not considered his.
misquoted_or_legend.source: New Catholic Encyclopedia: 'The confessio formerly attributed to him is not considered authentic.'

misquoted_or_legend.claim: Translation slips in Roberts that can pass into copy: baptised 'of the age of twenty years'; served 'under king Constantine'; 'as long as Martin survived' (Sacred History 2.50).
misquoted_or_legend.truth: The Latin says eighteen ('annorum duodeviginti'), Constantius ('sub rege Constantio'), and 'as long as Martin was at Trier' ('quoad usque Martinus Treveris fuit').
misquoted_or_legend.source: Halm's Latin text at The Latin Library (Vita Martini; Chronica II)

where_he_stood.text: Ten of the quiz's 23 statements. Five show a line and five are on record but not quoted. All are 'as Sulpicius Severus, who knew him, recorded it'. Values from site/src/data/which-early-christian.json (people.martin.cells). In the quiz's order:

rows.statement: A good hearty laugh is good for the soul.
rows.line: No one ever saw him enraged, or excited, or lamenting, or laughing.
rows.note: The line is cut short with a full stop (excerpt 'stop'). In Roberts a semicolon follows.

rows.statement: If you had to choose, you'd grow closer to God alone in quiet than among other people.
rows.line: Martin was accustomed to say to you, that such an abundance of power was by no means granted him while he was a bishop, as he remembered to have possessed before he obtained that office.
rows.note: Gallus is speaking to Sulpicius, so the 'you' is Sulpicius (VERIFY.md). Roberts has a footnote mark after 'abundance'.

rows.statement: If someone you know is doing wrong, it's your job to tell them.
rows.line: On record in Dialogues, not quoted.
rows.note: The research ties this to his rebuke of Brictio for keeping horses and buying slaves (Dialogue III, chapter 15).

rows.statement: The best way to live is free of strong emotions, with only a steady peace inside.
rows.line: No one ever saw him enraged, or excited, or lamenting, or laughing; he was always one and the same: displaying a kind of heavenly happiness in his countenance, he seemed to have passed the ordinary limits of human nature.

rows.statement: Your body is a friend to look after, not an enemy to fight.
rows.line: It is not fitting that a Christian should die except among ashes; and I have sinned if I leave you a different example.

rows.statement: God still speaks to people through dreams.
rows.line: On record in Life of St Martin, not quoted.
rows.note: The research: the dream of Christ in the cloak (chapter 3), and his testing of a false vision (chapter 24).

rows.statement: Miracles still happen today, just as they did in the Bible.
rows.line: On record in Dialogues, not quoted.
rows.note: The research: his healings and the Dialogue II chapter 4 saying.

rows.statement: A church should keep out people who openly live in serious wrongdoing.
rows.line: On record in Dialogues, not quoted.
rows.note: The research: he refused communion with the bishops behind the executions (Dialogue III, chapters 11-13).

rows.statement: A Christian can fight in a just war with a clear conscience.
rows.line: I am the soldier of Christ: it is not lawful for me to fight.

rows.statement: Governments should use their laws to promote the Christian faith.
rows.line: On record in Sacred History, not quoted.
rows.note: The research: 'a foul and unheard-of indignity, that a secular ruler should be judge in an ecclesiastical cause' (Book 2, chapter 50).

where_he_stood.source: site/src/data/which-early-christian.json; statement texts from the same file

how_he_died.text: He died of a fever in old age, at Candes in his own diocese, on 8 November 397. He had gone there to make peace among the local clergy. He died lying on sackcloth and ashes, praying, with his eyes on heaven. He was buried at Tours three days later.
how_he_died.source: Sulpicius, Letter 3 ('for some days under the influence of a strong fever'; 'upon sackcloth and ashes'); Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks 1.48; New Catholic Encyclopedia; OCA
how_he_died.note: He was about 81 by Gregory of Tours's count ('the eighty-first year of his life'). Sulpicius did not see it himself and relays those who were there.

is_he_a_saint.text: Yes, in the Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches, and Lutherans remember him too. Catholics keep 11 November. The Orthodox call him Martin the Merciful and keep 12 November (Greek), 12 October (Russian, old calendar) or 11 November (OCA). The Church of England and the Episcopal Church keep 11 November, and so does the Missouri Synod's Lutheran Service Book. He was honoured as a saint from the first, one of the first who did not die a martyr.
is_he_a_saint.source: USCCB; 1916 Roman Martyrology; OCA; synaxarion.gr; azbyka.ru; Church of England Common Worship; Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022; LSB via goodshepherd.nb.ca and LCMS Lutheran Witness; Britannica
is_he_a_saint.note: The 1916 Roman Martyrology entry for 11 November, exact: 'At Tours in France, the birthday of blessed Martin, bishop and confessor, whose life was so renowned for miracles that he received the power to raise three persons from the dead.' ELCA is not checked in an ELCA document.

what_to_read_first.text: The Life of St Martin, by Sulpicius Severus, who knew him. It was written while Martin was alive, is short, and is the source of almost everything.
what_to_read_first.note: Same translation, revised, at New Advent: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3501.htm . The Latin: https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/sulpiciusseverusmartin.html . The New Catholic Encyclopedia and the research say it was written in his lifetime. Letter 2 has Sulpicius dreaming, on the day news of the death came, that Martin 'held out in his right hand the small treatise which I had written concerning his life'.

what_to_read_first.text: Sulpicius's Letters 1 to 3. Letter 3 tells how he died.
The Dialogues: friends trading stories about Martin (Dialogues II and III).
Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks, Book 1, chapters 36 and 48: his birth, his death and the fight over his body, from a later bishop of Tours.
what_to_read_first.source: Ernest Brehaut (tr.), 1916, abridged, Fordham Medieval Sourcebook
what_to_read_first.note: Gregory wrote nearly two centuries later and ran Martin's shrine, so treat his extra stories as late.

eastern_icon.text: Saint Martin, an icon of the Cretan-Venetian school, about 1500 (first quarter of the 16th century). Tempera on wood, 35 x 28.3 cm. Petit Palais, Paris, PPP4870 (bequest of Roger Cabal, 1998). It shows him on horseback cutting his cloak for the beggar, with the hand of God above, and a Latin inscription 'S(ANCTUS) (M)ARTINU(S)'.
eastern_icon.licence: Public domain. The museum releases the image as CC0 (Paris Musées); Commons tags it PD-old-100-expired with a CC0 release.
eastern_icon.source: Paris Musées collections record; Wikimedia Commons
eastern_icon.note: Honest caption: an icon painted in Venetian Crete, in the Byzantine manner. The museum says the Latin inscription shows its patron was probably an Italian Catholic, and calls the piece probably unique among Cretan-Venetian icons. So it is Eastern in style, not an icon from Orthodox church use. Museum page: https://www.parismuseescollections.paris.fr/fr/petit-palais/oeuvres/saint-martin . Suggested credit: 'Saint Martin, Cretan-Venetian school, about 1500. Petit Palais, Paris. Paris Musées, CC0.'

personality_test.text: The site's own reading: Martin is one of the saints on the card for The Oak ('Sure of yourself, and at your best when life is quiet.'). The Oak is the confident, quiet type. The confident temper is read as settled steadiness and authority, never pride. His picture also stands for The Giver line ('who cut his cloak in two for a freezing beggar').
personality_test.oak_card_text: At court everyone flattered the emperor, and the bishops gave way. But “in Martin alone, apostolic authority continued to assert itself.” No one ever saw him angry or excited: “he was always one and the same.” When crowds of visitors grew too much for him, he moved to a hidden cell outside the city.
personality_test.oak_card_src: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St Martin
personality_test.note: Every claim on the card checks out against Roberts. Flattery and the bishops giving way: Life 20. 'in Martin alone, apostolic authority continued to assert itself': Life 20, exact. 'angry or excited' paraphrases 'enraged, or excited': Life 27. 'he was always one and the same': Life 27, exact. The hidden cell: Life 10. The Giver's 'freezing' fits Life 3 ('the extreme cold was proving fatal to many'). Say it is the site's reading, not Sulpicius's. The URL follows the route site/src/pages/personality-type/[slug].astro (slug = type key); the live page was not opened.

site_data_flags.text: people.martin.who says 'the best loved saint of Gaul'. That superlative has no direct source.
site_data_flags.note: The nearest sources: the Catholic Encyclopedia (1910), 'The Church of France has always considered Martin one of her greatest saints'; Brehaut, that Tours had become 'the religious metropolis' of Gaul through Martin's legend; Farrar, in Roberts's introduction, 'his name was known from Armenia to Egypt more widely than that of any other monk or bishop of his day'. Consider 'one of the best loved saints of Gaul'.

site_data_flags.text: The research status_note says 'one of the first saints honoured in the West who was not a martyr'. Britannica says 'one of the first nonmartyrs to be publicly venerated as a saint', with no 'in the West'.
The research misattributed list names the citizen 'Ruricius' (Roberts). The Latin and the Catholic Encyclopedia have 'Rusticius'.

The research genuine_lines are New Advent's revised wording (you/your). If the site prints Roberts, use the unrevised forms above. The two lines already on the site ('war', 'body') are the same in both.

could_not_verify: GOARCH's date for Martin. goarch.org returned 403 and then a bot check, which I did not get round. The Greek date of 12 November is confirmed from synaxarion.gr and saint.gr instead.
ELCA (Evangelical Lutheran Worship) listing '11 November, Martin, Bishop of Tours, died 397'. Seen only on Wikipedia and in a synod video title, not in an ELCA document.
That Clare Stancliffe (1983) prefers 336 as his birth year. Seen only in Wikipedia's note. The New Catholic Encyclopedia confirms that scholars differ.
Patronages beyond France, soldiers and tailors (Wikipedia's list: beggars, geese, innkeepers, vintners, horses, Buenos Aires, Utrecht, Szombathely and others).
The goose and the globe of fire as art attributes. Where the 'half the cloak belonged to the army' explanation comes from. When the goose legend began.
An ancient source for the day '8 November'. Modern references agree. Gregory of Tours gives the year, a Sunday and midnight, and 8 November 397 was a Sunday by my calculation.
The date of the Ravenna mosaic (5th century on Commons, c. 560 in the research).
The current (2004) Roman Martyrology's wording. Only the 1916 English edition was checked.
